questions.q: Phenol (in excess) condenses with formaldehyde in acid to give polymer A. Heating A with more formaldehyde (or hexamethylenetetramine) gives a thermosetting polymer B. A and B are
questions.explain: Phenol in excess gives the linear, thermoplastic prepolymer novolac; extra –CH₂– bridges from more HCHO cross-link it into bakelite.

questions.q: Unbreakable crockery is made from a condensation polymer of formaldehyde with
questions.explain: Melamine–formaldehyde resin (Melmac) is used for unbreakable crockery; urea–formaldehyde resin is matched with laminated sheets and phenol–formaldehyde (bakelite) with electrical switches.

questions.q: Which statement about formaldehyde resins is INCORRECT?
options: Bakelite is a cross-linked thermosetting polymer
Urea–formaldehyde resin is a condensation polymer with –NH–CH₂–NH– links
Formaldehyde attacks phenol at the ortho and para positions
Novolac is formed when formaldehyde is in excess over phenol
questions.explain: Novolac forms with phenol in excess (F:P less than 1). The base-catalysed resole route is the one with formaldehyde in excess.

questions.q: Why can phenol form a three-dimensional network with formaldehyde, while a ring with only two reactive positions would give only linear chains?
options: The –OH group activates two ortho and one para position, so each ring can carry up to three –CH₂– bridges
Phenol reacts with HCHO at the meta positions, which are the most activated
Each formaldehyde molecule forms three –CH₂– bridges
Phenol undergoes addition polymerisation through its ring C=C bonds
questions.explain: When each ring uses only two positions the chain stays linear (novolac); using the third free ortho/para position links neighbouring chains, giving cross-linked bakelite.
